title: Graphs & networks
examples: What is the difference between an edge and a vertex?
How do I check if a graph has an Eulerian path?
Can you give an example of a graph with no edges?

explain.say: Today we learn about graphs and networks. A graph has points and lines connecting them. These points are called vertices. The lines connecting them are called edges.
The degree of a vertex is the count of edges connected to it. If a vertex has four edges, its degree is four. Think of it like counting connections.

draw.text: Degree = count of edges at a vertex

explain.say: An Eulerian path uses every edge exactly once. It is like traversing every street in a town once. A graph can have such a path if it has zero or two vertices with an odd degree.

items: Eulerian path: uses every edge once
Requires zero or two odd degree vertices

draw.text: Eulerian Path: Use every edge once

explain.say: A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex exactly once. It is like a tour visiting every city once. This is harder to check than the Eulerian path.

draw.text: Hamiltonian Cycle: Visit every vertex once

faq.q: What is the difference between an Eulerian path and a Hamiltonian path?
faq.a: An Eulerian path uses every edge exactly once. A Hamiltonian path visits every vertex exactly once. You are counting edges for the first, and vertices for the second.
asks: Does it use all the lines or all the dots?
Which one is about edges and which one is about vertices?

faq.q: If all vertices have an even degree, what kind of path exists?
faq.a: If all vertices have an even degree, the graph has an Eulerian circuit. This means you can start and end at the same vertex after using every edge once.
asks: What if the start and end point are the same?
Does this mean it's a cycle?

faq.q: Is it always possible to find a Hamiltonian cycle?
faq.a: No, it is not always possible. Checking for a Hamiltonian cycle is much more difficult than checking for an Eulerian path.
asks: Is there a simple rule for Hamiltonian cycles?
Is it as easy as the Eulerian path?

faq.q: What is the minimum number of edges needed for a graph?
faq.a: A graph can have zero edges if it only has vertices. If it has edges, it must have at least one edge connecting two vertices.
asks: Can a graph exist with no lines?
What is the smallest graph with edges?

faq.q: Can a graph have more than two vertices with an odd degree?
faq.a: No, a graph can have at most two vertices with an odd degree. This is a fundamental rule in graph theory.
asks: How many odd degree vertices can there be?
Must the number of odd vertices be even?

facts: A graph consists of a set of vertices and a set of edges.
The degree of a vertex is the number of edges incident to it.
A graph has an Eulerian path if it has zero or exactly two vertices of odd degree.
A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex exactly once and returns to the start.

quiz.say: In a graph, the number of edges connected to a single point is called its:
quiz.why: The degree specifically counts the number of edges attached to that single vertex.

wrong.1: A vertex is the point itself, not the count of lines on it.
wrong.2: A cycle describes a path, not the count of connections at one point.
wrong.3: This is too general; the specific mathematical term is degree.

quiz.say: If a graph has exactly two vertices with an odd degree, what kind of path is possible?
quiz.why: Exactly two odd vertices allow you to start at one and end at the other, using every edge once.

wrong.0: A circuit requires all vertices to have an even degree, which is not guaranteed here.
wrong.1: Having two odd vertices guarantees the existence of such a path.
wrong.3: This path requires visiting every vertex once, which is a different concept.

quiz.say: A path that visits every single vertex exactly once is called a:
quiz.why: The definition of a Hamiltonian path is visiting every vertex exactly one time.

wrong.1: An Eulerian path focuses on using every edge exactly once, not every vertex.
wrong.2: A circuit implies returning to the starting vertex, which is not required here.
wrong.3: This describes a calculation, not the type of path taken.
